page: Google Cloud Platform t2a-standard-48 is an ARM-based server instance powered by the t2a family. It features 48 dedicated physical cores using the ARMv8 Neoverse-N1 architecture running at 3.0 GHz, with 1.0 thread per core. The instance is equipped with 192.0 GB of system memory, providing a balanced 4.0 GB of RAM per core. It does not include local NVMe storage or GPU accelerators, relying entirely on network-attached storage.

Benchmark data reveals strong multi-core capabilities, with stress-ng multi-core CPU performance reaching 87022.37 and Redis SET operations achieving 61.65 million operations per second. However, single-core performance is a relative bottleneck; the Geekbench single-core score of 1110.0 and single-threaded bzip3 decompression of 8.87 GB/sec fall into the lower performance tiers. Memory bandwidth is stable, with cached small-block reads at 3391.09 GB/sec and uncached large-block writes at 78.56 GB/sec.

The ARMv8 architecture lacks x86-specific instruction sets such as AVX, AVX-512, and AMX, which limits its utility for heavy vector math or advanced matrix operations. LLM text generation benchmarks reflect this, showing weak performance on larger models. Qualitatively, the dedicated physical cores and high core density offer predictable multi-threaded scaling and cost-efficient throughput for workloads that parallelize well, making it a viable alternative to traditional x86 instances for scale-out architectures.

This instance is suited for multi-threaded applications, Redis caching layers, static web serving, software compilation, and general-purpose containerized microservices. It is less suitable for single-threaded legacy applications or large-scale AI inference tasks.

It is configured with 192.0 GB of RAM, translating to 4.0 GB per core, and contains no local storage or GPU accelerators. Performance benchmarks indicate strong multi-core scaling, highlighted by 87022.37 in stress-ng multi-core tests and 61.65 million operations per second in Redis SET operations. Conversely, single-core performance is relatively weak, as shown by a Geekbench single-core score of 1110.0. Lacking AVX and AMX instruction sets, this instance is not designed for heavy vector math. It provides a cost-efficient, high-density platform for parallelized workloads, making it highly suitable for multi-threaded applications, web serving, software compilation, and database operations, while remaining less optimal for single-threaded tasks or large-scale language model inference.
